opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is one of the places where TensorLogic actually has an advantage, even though people often assume a higher-level language must cost you efficiency.

The core construct in TensorLogic is the tensor equation, which is essentially an Einstein summation. A logical rule is a join followed by a projection, and in tensor terms that's multiplying tensors and summing out the indices that don't appear on the left-hand side. So everything you write reduces to one very regular kind of operation. That's good news for optimization, because instead of a compiler having to understand a zoo of arbitrary Python code, it only has to be very good at one thing: executing einsums, dense or sparse, as fast as possible on the hardware you have.

That gives you a clean separation of concerns. The person writing the model says *what* they want to compute, and the system decides *how*: which order to contract the tensors in, whether to treat something as dense or sparse, how to tile it, how to fuse operations, how to distribute it across GPUs. Databases solved a version of this decades ago. Nobody hand-writes the join order in SQL; the query optimizer does it, and it often does better than people would. TensorLogic can inherit a lot of that machinery, plus everything that's been done on einsum contraction ordering and kernel generation for GPUs.

Sparsity is a good example of where this matters. Symbolic knowledge tends to be extremely sparse. Most facts are false. Neural representations are dense. In TensorLogic they're the same kind of object, so the system can pick the representation per tensor, and even convert between them, without the programmer rewriting anything. If you tried to do that by hand in PyTorch you'd end up with two codebases glued together.

Now, there will always be cases where somebody wants to squeeze out the last few percent with a hand-tuned kernel, and I don't think the language should forbid that. You should be able to annotate things, give hints, or drop down to a lower level for a particular operation, the way you can call a C routine from a high-level language. But that should be the exception. The history of computing is that once compilers get good enough, the high-level approach wins, because the productivity gain is enormous and the performance gap shrinks to almost nothing. I'd expect the same here. And because the language is so small and uniform, I think it's actually easier to get the compiler to that point than it has been for general-purpose languages.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, that's actually one of the main motivations for Tensor Logic in the first place. The whole idea is that logical inference and tensor algebra are really the same thing underneath. A Datalog rule, a join followed by a projection, is just an Einstein summation, a contraction over shared indices. So once you write everything in that language, you inherit all the machinery that's been built up for tensors over the last fifteen years: GPUs, TPUs, kernel fusion, the compilers like XLA and Triton, autodiff. You don't have to reinvent any of that. The logic sits on top of the same substrate the neural nets run on.

Now, people sometimes push back and say, well, but symbolic structures are sparse, and if you turn a knowledge base into a dense tensor you blow up memory and compute. That's true if you do it naively. But the right way to think about it is that density and sparsity are implementation decisions, not semantic ones. The program says what to compute; the compiler decides how. Sparse tensor formats, hashing, indexing, the kind of thing a database query optimizer does, all of that becomes the job of the compiler rather than something the programmer has to worry about. And in fact the database community and the tensor community have been converging on this for a while. Worst-case optimal join algorithms and contraction ordering for tensor networks are basically the same problem.

So my view is that Tensor Logic should be a high-level language, in the same sense that Python or Prolog are, and the low-level optimization lives in a compiler layer underneath. If anything, having a single uniform representation makes optimization easier, because today you have this awkward boundary where you call out of PyTorch into some symbolic reasoner and back, and nothing can be optimized across that boundary. If it's all one computation graph, the compiler can see the whole thing.

Does that mean a hand-tuned CUDA kernel will always lose to a Tensor Logic program? No, not today. But that was true of C versus assembly once too, and we all know how that turned out. The abstraction wins because the optimizations get built once and everybody gets them.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to separate the level at which you express the computation from the level at which you execute it. You want to describe your model or your reasoning in a clear, high-level way, but that doesn’t mean the implementation has to be naive. The compiler should be able to take that description and turn it into very efficient code.

With TensorLogic, there are opportunities on both sides. On the logical side, you can reorder operations, exploit sparsity, and avoid computing things that aren’t needed. On the tensor side, you can use things like operation fusion, efficient memory layouts, and hardware-specific kernels. Ideally, the compiler considers those together, because a transformation that looks good algebraically might be bad for memory traffic, and vice versa.

And you still want an escape hatch. If somebody has a highly optimized implementation of a particular operation, they should be able to plug it in. The point of a high-level language is to make those optimizations reusable, so that everybody doesn’t have to rediscover them and write them by hand.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to separate the language in which you express the computation from the way that computation is executed. You want to describe the model and the reasoning at a high level, but that doesn’t mean you have to give up control over efficiency. The compiler should be able to choose representations, exploit sparsity, fuse operations, and map the computation onto the hardware.

And when you need a particularly optimized implementation of some operation, you should be able to plug that in. You shouldn’t have to express every low-level detail in TensorLogic itself. The idea is to give you a unified framework in which those optimizations can happen, while preserving the high-level meaning of the program. Of course, making the compiler good enough to deliver on that is a substantial engineering challenge.
